Yep — this is a basic CareerConnect home/dashboard page. The overall purpose is: - show the user’s name in the header - display a top navigation bar - render a few “tiles” for features like jobs, CVs, applications, and favourites - redirect back to the login page if no user is stored in localStorage Quick breakdown of the important parts: - Header: -
contains the brand + navigation - The username is inserted into - Nav links: - "Home" is marked active - other links are placeholders with href="#" so they don’t go anywhere yet - the “My Tools” section is a dropdown menu - Main content: -
contains a welcome message and tiles - the tiles are simple cards with icons and labels - Authentication check: - const name = localStorage.getItem("userName"); - if a name exists, it is shown - otherwise, it does: window.location.href = "index.html"; That last part is important — it means the page only works if the user logged in before and saved their name in localStorage. One small thing to notice: - The page uses external CSS: - The navigation for “Postings”, “Messages”, etc. is currently just placeholder links, so they’ll need real pages or JS later If your question is more specific, like: - “How do I make the dropdown work?” - “How do I fix login redirect?” - “How do I add a jobs page?” - “Can you rewrite this cleaner?” I can help with that directly.

Exactly — in HTML, `class="page"` does not mean “there is a class object being instantiated” like in JavaScript or C++.

This is the key difference:

- In HTML, `class` is just an attribute on an element
- It’s used to group elements together
- Those names are then matched by CSS (and sometimes JS), not by a language runtime

So this:

```html
<main class="page">
```

means:

- “This `<main>` element belongs to the group named `page`”
- Then somewhere in CSS, there is probably something like:

```css
.page {
  padding: 2rem;
  max-width: 1200px;
  margin: 0 auto;
}
```

That CSS selector `.page` targets all elements with `class="page"`.

Likewise:

```html
<header class="topbar">
```

matches:

```css
.topbar {
  ...
}
```

and:

```html
<div class="dropdown">
```

matches:

```css
.dropdown {
  ...
}
```

So no, HTML classes are not like C++ classes or JavaScript classes in the OOP sense.

They are more like labels or hooks.

Important distinctions:

- HTML: `class` attribute
- CSS: `.class-name { ... }` selector
- JavaScript: `document.querySelector(".page")` or `document.getElementsByClassName("page")`

Also note: the `class` attribute can be used on multiple elements at once, and the same element can have multiple classes:

```html
<div class="page card featured">
```

Then CSS can target any of them individually:

```css
.page { ... }
.card { ... }
.featured { ... }
```

So your instinct is good: in HTML/CSS, the “class” concept is not a class definition like in programming languages. It’s just a way to style or select page elements.

In your file specifically, the `class="page"` is almost certainly defined in the linked stylesheet:
`css/style.css`

That stylesheet is where you’ll find selectors like:

```css
.page { ... }
```

and not a JS or C++ class definition.

If you want, I can also show you exactly how to read the HTML/CSS relationship in this project and point out where the `.page`, `.topbar`, etc. are likely defined in the stylesheet.
